newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: SOCCER-URUGUAY DEPART AFTER ANOTHER FAILURE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-URUGUAY DEPART AFTER ANOTHER FAILURE.

text.p: Defending champions Uruguay left Bolivia Friday following a first round Copa America elimination which represents another international failure for a country that used to be one of soccer's major powers.

Uruguay have won the Copa America 13 times and the World Cup twice, a tremendous record for a nation of only four million people, but their recent soccer history has been one of a seemingly unstoppable decline into obscurity.

They failed to qualify for the last World Cup and are in danger of not reaching the 1998 tournament in France either. Their triumph in the last Copa America, which they hosted two years ago, seems to have had brought no long-term benefit.

Only four of the 12 Copa America teams were knocked out in the first round but the once mighty Uruguayans were one of them with their only points coming in a 2-0 win over minnows Venezuela. Their other results included a 1-0 defeat by a young, inexperienced Peruvian team.

Uruguay had a chance of going through as one of the two best third-placed teams but were edged out on goals scored by Colombia, who qualified despite losing 2-0 to Brazil on Thursday to go through in their place.

"Uruguay are still on the road to France and what has happened in the Copa America is part of the past," said beleagured coach Juan Ahuntchain, who replaced Hector Nunez halfway through the World Cup qualifying campaign.

Uruguay will return to Bolivia for a World Cup qualifier in July and plan to arrive 20 days in advance to acclimatise to the altitude. The city lies at 3,600 metres above seal level and the thin air makes it a nightmare venue for visiting teams.

Inevitably for a soccer coach whose team is performing badly, Ahuntchain has found himself under intense pressure, with his future the subject of much speculation. "We'll talk about my future when we get back to Montevideo," he said.
Meanwhile, the battle continued for the other teams.

Colombia, who scraped through as the second best third-placed team, have been rewarded with a quarter-final in La Paz Saturday against the hosts less than 48 hours after completing their last game against Brazil -- hardly time to adapt to the unusual conditions in the capital.

The team, who played their first round games at sea level in Santa Cruz, will arrive just hours before kick-off. The short time given for teams to adapt to high altitude venues has been one of the main criticisms of the way the Copa America has been organised.
Peru and Argentina meet in Sucre at 2,700 metres earlier Saturday, with Ecuador playing Mexico in Cochabamba at 2,600 metres Sunday.
The most attractive game is between world champions Brazil and Paraguay, leaders of the South American World Cup qualifying group, in Santa Cruz Sunday.

The Paraguayans were busy Friday denying rumours that some of the players had a night out on the town in Cochabamba before their last game. "This is something the press invented and the whole squad has been tarred," said goalkeeper Jose Luis Chilavert. "I would put my hand in the fire for my team-mates."
